problems.stem: A showcase plan is judged a success because 'the room was packed all session.' What is the strongest critique?
options: It is a success; a packed room means engagement.
Foot traffic is not the goal; the goal is visitors seeing theory-to-screen reasoning and presenters getting substantive questions.
It would be better with even more visitors.
Success should be measured by how long visitors stayed.
problems.explanation: A showcase is an evidence exchange; crowd size does not show that design reasoning was communicated.

problems.stem: Visitors keep asking only 'cool, what is it?' and never see the README traceability matrix. What change surfaces the design reasoning?
options: Make the prototypes look more impressive.
Post a per-station card: 'Ask me which screen changed because of which theory.'
Hand visitors a longer printed program.
Add background music to the room.
problems.explanation: A focusing prompt makes the traceability matrix the conversation rather than an afterthought.

problems.stem: An organizer uses AI to draft the rotation schedule. What is the strongest boundary?
options: Accept the AI schedule unchecked because it looks organized.
Use the AI draft, then verify against the real constraint: 8 stations, 50 minutes, no prototype mobbed or skipped.
Skip scheduling and let visitors wander.
Ask AI only to make the schedule look more colorful.
problems.explanation: AI can propose a schedule, but the organizer must check it against the room's actual logistics constraints.

problems.stem: After switching to timed rotations with staggered starts, which result best shows the change worked?
options: Every prototype received visitors in both rounds and presenters logged questions about specific README matrix rows.
More visitors signed the guest book.
The room stayed full until the end.
problems.explanation: Balanced visits plus substantive theory-to-screen questions are the auditable evidence of an evidence exchange.
